initial_summary: Gene expression levels vary significantly between individuals, and these differences can influence traits related to evolution and disease. (E001) While researchers understand how DNA changes upstream of genes affect expression, the role of RNA 3′-end processing—the mechanism that determines where a transcript stops—remains less understood. (E002, E017) This process, known as alternative polyadenylation, determines the length of the 3′ untranslated region, which controls a transcript's stability, translation, and location within a cell. (E006, E011) To investigate this, researchers developed a high-throughput sequencing approach to precisely measure the ends of mRNA transcripts and identify functional regulatory elements across six human cell lines. (E012, E018, E019) The study analyzed whether genetic variations in polyadenylation signals and other 3′ motifs are associated with changes in total gene expression levels. (E020, E025) The researchers found that transcript end positions are not random but are located near specific regulatory sites, such as microRNA binding regions. (E003) Genetic differences between individuals contribute to variations in 3′-end processing, particularly in immune-related genes. (E022, E023) Variations in polyadenylation signals can force the production of transcripts that are less stable or processed less efficiently, leading to lower total gene expression. (E007, E024) The choice between short and long transcript forms determines which regulatory elements, such as Pumilio sites, are included in the final mature mRNA. (E009, E010, E013, E021) These sequence differences in polyadenylation signals are a key mechanism explaining why gene expression levels vary between individual humans. (E004, E008, E014) Because these variations can influence the risk of both rare and common diseases, models of gene expression are incomplete if they do not account for 3′-end processing. (E005, E015) A complete understanding of human genetics requires integrating these processing signals with the sequence elements that control the ultimate fate of the transcript. (E016)

reference: Messenger RNAs carry the instructions necessary to synthesize proteins that do work for the cell . Extending beyond the protein-coding sequence of a given mRNA is an additional stretch of sequence , harboring signals that govern how much protein is made and how long the mRNA remains in the cell before it is broken down . The incorporation of this end region into mature mRNA is itself subject to change; for the vast majority of human genes , how and why cells use different mRNA ends remains largely unknown . In this work , we surveyed mRNA ends from ∼10 , 000 genes in immune cells from genetically distinct human individuals . We found that mRNA end positions were not randomly distributed , but rather preferentially flanked the locations of regulatory signals that govern mRNA fate . The usage of these mRNA length forms and regulatory elements varied across individuals and could be dissected molecularly . Our results uncover key mechanisms and regulatory effects of transcript end processing , particularly as these are perturbed by genetic differences between humans .

initial_summary: The live attenuated simian immunodeficiency virus (SIV) vaccine, known as SIVΔnef, is highly effective at protecting against wild-type lentiviral challenges, including mucosal and heterologous viral strains. Researchers used next-generation sequencing to examine how the virus evolved in 12 rhesus macaques after they were vaccinated with this weakened version of the virus. The study found that the SIVΔnef vaccine undergoes sequence evolution and viral escape during the vaccination period, even when viral replication levels are low. The virus frequently develops mutations to escape the immune system's CD8 T cell responses, particularly in highly variable regions of its genome. Between 5 and 20 weeks after vaccination, the CD8 T cell immune response shifts its focus to different parts of the virus. This process, called anentropic specificity, causes the immune response to shift toward targeting highly conserved and stable viral regions, such as the Gag and Pol proteins. By 20 weeks post-vaccination, the immune system focuses more on these stable parts rather than regions that change easily, regardless of the animal's genetic background. While immune responses targeting variable regions decline as the virus mutates, responses targeting stable regions are maintained over time. The vaccine also generates new, de novo immune responses to viral variants that have escaped previous detection, a process termed 'deepening' of the immune repertoire. SIVΔnef acts as a persistent vaccine that evolves alongside the immune response, helping to shape and mature the body's defenses. Researchers hypothesize that the efficacy of live-attenuated vaccines depends on this viral evolution to redirect immune targeting toward conserved regions. Increased vaccine protection correlates with this broader and deeper CD8 T cell repertoire that targets stable parts of the virus. These findings provide a model for successful HIV vaccine design, suggesting that future vaccines should focus T cells on conserved viral regions and their known variants.

reference: Annually , more than two million people are infected with HIV , the virus that causes AIDS . Due to the ability of the virus to escape host immune responses , designing a successful HIV vaccine has been elusive . Similar to HIV in humans , rhesus macaques can be infected with SIV , a close relative and ancestor of HIV , resulting in simian AIDS . SIVΔnef , a live attenuated form of SIV , protects rhesus macaques from subsequent challenge with pathogenic SIV and is widely viewed as the most effective SIV vaccine . Here , we demonstrate that after vaccination of macaques with SIVΔnef , the immune response initially targets more variable regions of the virus , which the virus rapidly escapes . However , as the virus escapes , the immune response evolves to target more conserved regions of the virus as well as escape variants . This refocused targeting of conserved regions by the immune response provides a new mechanistic model that contributes to our understanding of how SIVΔnef vaccination protects animals from pathogenic challenge with SIV . Our findings also reinforce the importance of developing HIV vaccines that target conserved regions of the virus as well as their potential variants .

initial_summary: Mucosal infections caused by the fungus Candida albicans are common, but the mechanisms the body uses to trigger antifungal immunity are not fully understood. Researchers used a mouse model of oral candidiasis to investigate how the immune system recruits neutrophils, which are white blood cells essential for controlling fungal growth and spread. While the IL-17 pathway is known to be important for fungal defense, this study found that the interleukin-1 receptor (IL-1R) pathway is the primary controller of neutrophil movement to the oral mucosa. The study utilized tongue-derived keratinocytes and blood endothelial cell lines to observe how different cell types communicate during an infection. Researchers also measured the expression of genes for inflammatory signals, such as IL-1α and IL-1β, and neutrophil-recruiting chemokines in tongue tissues. The results showed that IL-1R signaling is essential for recruiting existing neutrophils from the blood and triggering the production of new ones in the bone marrow. When live, invading fungal hyphae damage oral keratinocytes, these cells release IL-1α as an 'alarmin' to alert the host. This IL-1α signal prompts nearby blood endothelial cells to produce G-CSF, a growth factor that enters the bloodstream to reach the bone marrow. G-CSF then triggers 'emergency granulopoiesis,' a process that boosts the production and mobilization of neutrophils to meet the high demand caused by the infection. These findings demonstrate that a coordinated crosstalk between keratinocytes and endothelial cells is vital for protecting the body from Candida albicans.

reference: The opportunistic pathogen Candida albicans is a major risk factor for immunosuppressed individuals , and oropharyngeal candidiasis ( OPC ) is a frequent complication in patients with weakened cellular immunity . The cytokine interleukin-17 ( IL-17 ) plays a critical role for antifungal host defense and was proposed to act by regulating neutrophil recruitment to the oral mucosa . However , although IL-17 can promote neutrophil trafficking in some situations , we recently showed in a mouse model that this is not the case during OPC . Thus , the mechanism governing the neutrophil response to C . albicans remained to be determined . Here , we demonstrate an essential role of IL-1 receptor ( IL-1R ) signaling in the recruitment of neutrophils from the circulation to the infected tissue via enhanced secretion of chemokines and increased output of neutrophils from the bone marrow . We found that IL-1α is released from keratinocytes upon invasion of C . albicans and acts on endothelial cells to induce the production of granulocyte colony-stimulating factor ( G-CSF ) , a key trigger of emergency granulopoiesis . Thereby , IL-1R signaling translates the local response to the fungus in the oral mucosa into a systemic response that critically contributes to protection from infection .

initial_summary: Lymphatic filariasis is a parasitic infection that stands as a primary cause of permanent and long-term disability across the globe. To combat this, the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis (GPELF) was established in 2000 to provide annual mass drug administration to populations at risk. The program relies on long-term drug donations from pharmaceutical companies GlaxoSmithKline and Merck & Co., Inc., which are committed to providing these treatments until the disease is eliminated. By interrupting the transmission cycle, the program protects newborns and the general population from ever acquiring the infection. For those already infected, the treatment provides significant health benefits by halting the progression of the disease. During its first eight years, the GPELF generated an estimated total economic benefit of US$24.0 billion. This total includes US$21.8 billion in direct and indirect savings for treated individuals, consisting of US$1.4 billion in avoided treatment costs and US$20.4 billion in prevented lost wages. Additionally, national health systems in endemic countries saved approximately US$2.2 billion by reducing the need for patient services. Because essential drugs are donated at no cost, the financial return on investment for governments and donors is exceptionally high. The cost-benefit ratio of this program is comparable to or even better than other major global health initiatives, such as malaria control programs.

reference: Lymphatic filariasis ( LF ) , commonly known as ‘elephantiasis’ , is one of the world's most debilitating infectious diseases . In 83 countries worldwide , more than 1 . 3 billion people are at risk of infection with an estimated 120 million individuals already infected . A recent publication reviewing the health impact of the first 8 years of the Global Programme to Eliminate Lymphatic Filariasis ( GPELF ) demonstrated the enormous health benefits achieved in populations receiving annual mass drug administration ( MDA ) , as a result of infection prevented , disease progression halted , and ancillary treatment of co-infections . To date , however , no studies have estimated the economic value of these health benefits , either to the individuals or the societies afflicted with LF . Our study estimates that US$21 . 8 billion will be gained among individuals benefitting from just the first 8 years of the Global Programme , and an additional US$2 . 2 billion will be saved by the health systems of endemic countries . Treating endemic populations is possible at very low cost – particularly because of the generous drug donations from two pharmaceutical companies – but results in enormous economic benefits . Findings from this study yield a much clearer understanding the GPELF's full economic impact and strengthen the conviction that it is a ‘best buy’ in global health .

initial_summary: Gaucher disease is the most common lysosomal storage disorder and is caused by having two mutated copies of the GBA gene. While these mutations cause Gaucher disease, carrying even a single mutated GBA gene is a significant risk factor for developing sporadic Parkinson’s disease. To study this connection, researchers created a specific mutant medaka fish (GBAW337X/W337X) that lacks the glucocerebrosidase enzyme. Unlike human and mouse models with this deficiency that die shortly after birth, these medaka fish survive for more than three months. This extended lifespan allowed researchers to use the fish brains to study the progression of Gaucher disease and the expression of proteins like alpha-synuclein and APOE. The GBA-deficient medaka displayed symptoms similar to human neuronopathic Gaucher disease, including the loss of nerve cells and the presence of specialized "Gaucher-like" cells in the brain. The study found that the enzyme deficiency causes lysosomal dysfunction, which leads to the accumulation of waste materials and dysfunctional mitochondria. This dysfunction disrupts the transport of waste-degrading structures called autophagosomes, causing them to swell within nerve fibers. Alpha-synuclein, a protein closely linked to Parkinson's disease, was found to accumulate within these swollen autophagosomes in the fish brains. Surprisingly, removing the alpha-synuclein protein did not improve the fish's lifespan, movement, brain inflammation, or nerve cell loss. These findings establish GBA-deficient medaka as a viable model for studying how Gaucher disease progresses and how alpha-synuclein accumulation occurs in the brain.

reference: Parkinson’s disease ( PD ) is a neurodegenerative disease characterized by intraneuronal accumulation of alpha-synuclein ( α-syn ) called Lewy bodies and Lewy neurites . Recent genetic studies have revealed that mutations in glucocerebrosidase ( GBA ) , a causative gene of Gaucher disease ( GD ) , are a strong risk for PD . However , its pathological mechanisms leading to PD remain largely unknown . Here , we generated GBA nonsense mutant ( GBA-/- ) medaka which survive long enough for pathological analysis of disease progression . These mutant medaka display not only the phenotypes resembling human neuronopathic GD but also axonal accumulation of α-syn accompanied by impairment of the autophagy-lysosome pathway . Furthermore , the present study demonstrates this α-syn accumulation has negligible contribution to the pathogenesis of neuronopathic GD in medaka . GBA-/- medaka represent a valuable model for exploring the pathological mechanisms of PD with GBA mutations as well as neuronopathic GD , and our findings have important implications for the association of GBA mutations with PD .

initial_summary: Cell-fate reprogramming is a fundamental process in biological development where one cell type is converted into another. Researchers used C. elegans, a species of roundworm, as the model organism for this study. In the C. elegans germline, converting germ cells into somatic cells requires the disruption of chromatin, which is the material that packages DNA.

reference: The DNA in genes encodes the basic information needed to build an organism or control its day-to-day operations . Most cells in an organism contain the same genetic information , but different types of cell use the information differently . For example , many of the genes that are active in a muscle cell are different from those that are active in a skin cell . These different patterns of gene activation largely determine a cell’s identity and are brought about by DNA-binding proteins or chemical modifications to the DNA ( which are both forms of so-called epigenetic regulation ) . Nevertheless , cells occasionally change their identities – a phenomenon that is referred to as reprograming . This process allows tissues to be regenerated after wounding , but , due to technical difficulties , reprograming has been often studied in isolated cells grown in a dish . Seelk , Adrian-Kalchhauser et al . set out to understand how being surrounded by intact tissue influences reprograming . The experiments made use of C . elegans worms , because disturbing how this worm’s DNA is packaged can trigger its cells to undergo reprograming . Seelk , Adrian-Kalchhauser et al . show that a signaling pathway that is found in many different animals enhances this kind of reprograming in C . elegans . On the one hand , these findings help in understanding how epigenetic regulation can be altered by a specific tissue environment . On the other hand , the findings also suggest that abnormal signaling can result in altered epigenetic control of gene expression and lead to cells changing their identity . Indeed , increased signaling is linked to a major epigenetic mechanism seen in specific blood tumors , suggesting that the regulatory principles uncovered using this simple worm model could eventually provide insights into a human disease . A future challenge will be to determine precisely how the studied signaling pathway interacts with the epigenetic regulator that controls reprograming . Understanding this interaction in molecular detail could help to devise strategies for controlling reprograming . These strategies could in turn lead to treatments for people with conditions that cause specific cells types to be lost , such as Alzheimer’s disease or injuries .

initial_summary: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a major clinical pathogen that causes serious infections in the lungs, blood, liver, and bladder. This bacterium is a leading cause of infections acquired in hospitals and is increasingly difficult to treat because many strains have developed resistance to antibiotics. Neutrophils are the primary immune cells that act as first responders to fight off invading pathogens like K. pneumoniae. Researchers used a specific strain of K. pneumoniae to study how lung infections progress in mice that were genetically modified to lack a protein called SKAP2. The team measured the production of reactive oxygen species (ROS)—chemicals used by immune cells to kill bacteria—to determine if SKAP2 is necessary for this protective response. The study found that SKAP2 is essential for the immune system to protect the lungs, as mice lacking this protein had a 100-fold higher bacterial burden and were less able to control the infection. This failure to control the bacteria depends specifically on the absence of SKAP2 in immune cells derived from the bone marrow. While neutrophils were present at the site of infection, they could not effectively contain the bacteria without the SKAP2 protein. Specifically, neutrophils lacking SKAP2 failed to produce protective ROS when they encountered K. pneumoniae or when their surface receptors were stimulated. SKAP2 works by interacting with enzymes like Src family kinases to activate the signaling circuit required for ROS production. These findings suggest that the increased severity of lung infections in SKAP2-deficient mice is directly linked to the inability of their neutrophils to generate these germ-killing chemicals. While these results clarify how the immune system fights K. pneumoniae in mice, it is not yet known if SKAP2 plays the same critical role in the human immune response.

reference: Klebsiella pneumoniae is a type of bacteria that can cause life-threatening infections – including pneumonia , blood stream infections , and urinary tract infections – in hospitalized patients . These infections can be difficult to treat because some K . pneumoniae are resistant to antibiotics . The bacteria are normally found in the human intestine , and they do not usually cause infections in healthy people . This implies that healthy people’s immune systems are better able to fend off K . pneumoniae infections; learning how could help scientists develop new ways to treat or prevent infections in hospitalized patients . In healthy people , a type of immune cell called neutrophils are the first line of defense against bacterial infections . Several different proteins are needed to activate neutrophils , including a protein called SKAP2 . But the role of this protein in fighting K . pneumoniae infections is not clear . To find out what role SKAP2 plays in the defense against pneumonia caused by K . pneumoniae , Nguyen et al . compared infections in mice with and without the protein . Mice lacking SKAP2 in their white blood cells had more bacteria in their lungs than normal mice . The experiments showed that neutrophils from mice with SKAP2 produce a burst of chemicals called “reactive oxygen species” , which can kill bacteria . But neutrophils without the protein do not . Without SKAP2 , several proteins that help produce reactive oxygen species do not work . Understanding the role of SKAP2 in fighting infections may help scientists better understand the immune system . This could help clinicians to treat conditions that cause it to be hyperactive or ineffective . More studies are needed to determine if SKAP2 works the same way in human neutrophils and if it works against all types of K . pneumoniae . If it does , then scientists might be able use this information to develop therapies that help the immune system fight infections .

initial_summary: Plasmodium vivax is the most geographically widespread species of malaria, causing between 80 and 300 million clinical cases annually. A defining feature of this parasite is its ability to hide in the liver as dormant parasites called hypnozoites, which can activate weeks or months after the initial infection to cause new blood-stage infections known as relapses. These hypnozoites constitute a third parasite reservoir alongside the blood and mosquito reservoirs found in other malaria species like Plasmodium falciparum. Because standard malaria models do not account for this liver reservoir, they are not applicable to P. vivax. Researchers developed a mathematical model to simulate the transmission of P. vivax between humans and mosquitoes by accounting for the liver-stage reservoir. The model assumes that the number of hypnozoites in the liver increases with new mosquito bites and decreases when the parasites either activate to cause a relapse or die naturally. The researchers used individual patient data to estimate the time to the first relapse, though they had to make certain assumptions because the data were not sufficient to estimate all parameters simultaneously. The model predicts that the distribution of dormant liver parasites is highly uneven across a population, with some individuals carrying many parasites while others carry none. Individuals with a higher number of hypnozoites are predicted to experience more frequent relapses and a shorter time until their first relapse occurs. The model also suggests that relapses can occur immediately after the initial infection because hypnozoites activate at a constant rate. In temperate regions, the parasites exhibit a long-latency phase where they remain dormant for approximately six months before they are capable of activating. P. vivax is more difficult to control than P. falciparum because a single mosquito bite can cause multiple blood-stage infections through these relapses. Standard anti-malarial drugs like chloroquine target the blood reservoir but do not directly affect the liver-stage hypnozoites. The drug primaquine can clear both active blood infections and dormant liver-stage parasites. Including primaquine in first-line treatments is predicted to significantly reduce transmission because it targets the individuals most likely to relapse.

reference: Malaria is one of the world's most deadly infections , causing 100s of 1000s of deaths each year despite being both preventable and curable . Malaria is caused by Plasmodium parasites , which are transmitted between humans by mosquitoes . When a mosquito bites a human , Plasmodium is injected into the bloodstream with the mosquito's saliva . The parasite then travels through the bloodstream to the liver , infects liver cells and multiplies within those cells without causing any noticeable symptoms . After remaining silent in the liver for weeks or months , the now abundant parasite ruptures the host liver cell , re-enters the bloodstream , and begins infecting red blood cells . If another mosquito bites the infected individual and takes a blood meal , the parasite moves into the mosquito and the cycle of transmission continues . There are several species of Plasmodium that are known to cause malaria . The most widely studied species is P . falciparum , which also causes one of the deadliest types of malaria . However , another Plasmodium species called P . vivax is the most widely distributed species and , despite being less virulent than P . falciparum , is particularly dangerous because it causes recurring malaria . In contrast to P . falciparum , P . vivax has the ability to form hypnozoites: a dormant form of the parasite that can remain inside liver cells for long periods of time , sometimes for years . The reservoir of P . vivax hypnozoites can regularly populate the bloodstream with the infectious form of the parasite , triggering relapses of malaria . Even if an individual suffering a relapse receives prompt treatment to clear parasites in the blood , more parasites may emerge from the liver and cause new blood-stage infections . White et al . developed a mathematical model to help understand how P . vivax is transmitted . Unlike many of the established models of malaria transmission , the new model accounts for the reservoir of P . vivax hypnozoites in the liver , and assumes that hypnozoites in the reservoir either die , or are activated and enter the bloodstream , at a constant rate . This produces patterns that closely match how often relapses occur in patients . White et al . go on to predict that although many infected people have few or no hypnozoites in their liver , some have many hypnozoites , and these people are more likely to suffer from malaria relapses . This suggests that if the initial treatments given to malaria sufferers incorporate additional drugs that kill the hypnozoites in the liver , then it may be possible to substantially reduce the extent of P . vivax transmission .

initial_summary: Selective logging in the Amazon removes specific trees for timber, but unlike land cleared for farming, these forests remain standing and can eventually regain their lost carbon. This recovery process occurs through two main pathways: the continued growth of trees that survived the logging and the recruitment of new young trees. To understand how these forests bounce back, researchers used Bayesian hierarchical models to estimate changes in aboveground carbon stocks across the Amazon basin. The study specifically distinguished between the contributions of surviving trees and new recruits to model recovery trajectories. The researchers investigated how recovery is influenced by factors such as the intensity of the logging, the initial amount of carbon in the forest, annual rainfall, and soil density. Due to the length of available data from various experimental sites, the team focused their regional predictions on the first 10 years following the disturbance. The results show that trees surviving the logging are the primary drivers of carbon recovery across the entire Amazon. Immediately after logging, the recruitment of new trees increases significantly because there is less competition for sunlight and nutrients. Carbon recovery is highest in the Guiana Shield and western Amazon, where surviving trees grow back more vigorously. In contrast, the southern Amazon shows the lowest recovery rates because high environmental stress, including low rainfall and long dry seasons, limits tree growth. The speed of this recovery is also heavily dictated by the initial logging intensity and local environmental conditions like soil bulk density. Because many valuable timber species grow slowly, future wood stocks will depend almost entirely on the health and survival of the trees left behind after the first harvest.

reference: The Amazon rainforest in South America is the largest tropical forest in the world . Along with being home to a huge variety of plants and wildlife , rainforests also play an important role in storing an element called carbon , which is a core component of all life on Earth . Certain forms of carbon , such as the gas carbon dioxide , contribute to climate change so researchers want to understand what factors affect how much carbon is stored in rainforests . Trees and other plants absorb carbon dioxide from the atmosphere and then incorporate the carbon into carbohydrates and other biological molecules . The Amazon rainforest alone holds around 30% of the total carbon stored in land-based ecosystems . Humans selectively harvest certain species of tree that produce wood with commercial value from the Amazon rainforest . This “selective logging” results in the loss of stored carbon from the rainforest , but the loss can be compensated for in the medium to long term if the forest is left to regrow . New trees and trees that survived the logging grow to fill the gaps left by the felled trees . However , it is not clear how differences in the forest ( for example , forest maturity ) , environmental factors ( such as climate or soil ) and the degree of the disturbance caused by the logging affect the ability of the forest ecosystem to recover the lost carbon . Piponiot et al . used computer modeling to analyze data from over a hundred different forest plots across the Amazon rainforest . The models show that the forest’s ability to recover carbon after selective logging greatly differs between regions . For example , the overall amount of carbon recovered in the first ten years is predicted to be higher in a region in the north known as the Guiana Shield than in the south of the Amazonian basin where the climate is less favorable . The findings of Piponiot et al . highlight the key role the trees that survive selective logging play in carbon recovery . The next step would be to couple this model to historical maps of logging to estimate how the areas of the rainforest that are managed by selective logging shape the overall carbon balance of the Amazon rainforest .

initial_summary: Neural stem cells (NSCs) are found in two specific areas of the adult mammalian brain: the subgranular zone and the subventricular zone (SVZ). In the living brain, these stem cells persist throughout adulthood and produce essential brain cells, including neurons, astrocytes, and oligodendrocytes. Researchers have historically used 'neurosphere' formation in a lab dish as a proxy for neural stem cell function, but it has remained unclear if the cells that start these spheres are the actual long-lived stem cells. To investigate this, researchers isolated cells from the SVZ of adult mice and used flow cytometry to sort them into different groups based on 17 specific surface markers. The study utilized a combination of these markers to isolate and test two specific cell populations named GEPCOT and pre-GEPCOT cells. Isolated brain cells were tested for their ability to form neurospheres to measure their capacity to self-renew and differentiate into different cell types. The researchers identified two distinct populations in the SVZ: GEPCOT cells, which have high levels of EGFR and PlexinB2 proteins, and pre-GEPCOT cells. GEPCOT cells are highly active and divide frequently in the living brain, with nearly all cells dividing within a 24-hour period. However, these GEPCOT cells are short-lived and only persist transiently before being replaced. In contrast, pre-GEPCOT cells are quiescent, meaning they are dormant and do not divide frequently in the living brain. Unlike GEPCOT cells, pre-GEPCOT cells are unable to form neurospheres in laboratory cultures but are long-lived and survive chemotherapy-like treatments. Genetic markers and analysis of the SVZ and olfactory bulb confirmed that these quiescent pre-GEPCOT cells act as the true long-lived stem cells that replenish the active GEPCOT population. The ability to isolate these specific cell types using surface markers allows scientists to study how neural stem cells behave directly in living tissue rather than relying on artificial laboratory cultures.

reference: Neurons that arise in the adult nervous system originate from neural stem cells and neural progenitor cells . Neural stem cells have long lives , much of which they spend in a quiescent state . Neural stem cells can also give rise to neural progenitor cells , which proliferate rapidly during their short lives and then ‘differentiate’ into neurons or glia . Unlike some other tissues , it has not been possible to identify or purify neural stem cells directly from the tissue . Consequently , neural stem and progenitor cells have usually been studied retrospectively , based on their ability to form colonies in laboratory cell cultures . A region of the brain called the subventricular zone contains both neural stem cells and neural progenitor cells , and is one of only two regions of the brain where neural stem cells are found in adult mammals . When cells from the subventricular zone are cultured in a way that allows the cells to freely float around ( rather than growing on a surface ) , a few percent form spherical colonies called neurospheres . Since neurosphere-forming cells can self-renew and differentiate into neurons and glia , the ability of cells to form neurospheres has generally been taken as evidence that they are stem cells . However , the exact relationship between neural stem cells and neurosphere-forming cells has been uncertain . Now , Mich , Signer et al . have used a technique called flow cytometry to identify and isolate neural stem cells and neurosphere-forming cells directly from the subventricular zone . The neural stem cells , which Mich , Signer et al . term pre-GEPCOT cells ( based on an acronym of the markers used to isolate the cells ) , were long-lived and quiescent , but they lacked the ability to form colonies in culture . The neurosphere-forming cells , named GEPCOT cells , were short-lived and highly proliferative in the brain . These results demonstrate that the cells that form neurospheres in culture are not stem cells at all , and that real stem cells are not able to form colonies under existing culture conditions . The identification of undifferentiated pre-GEPCOT and GEPCOT cells will make it possible to directly study the properties of these cells inside the mouse brain , and to isolate live cells to test how they function . The results also highlight the need for new tests to study neural stem cell function , given that current tests using neurospheres do not detect stem cells as commonly assumed .
